title: Ancient writing systems and how they work

entries.note: Borrowed from French, from Vulgar Latin [[from:antianus]], from before, with an unetymological T added in Middle English; it meant the era before Rome's fall from about 1600.

entries.term: mustard in the style of the ancients
entries.translation: mustard in the style of the ancients
entries.note: The French name for wholegrain mustard, probably meaning in the olden style rather than the Roman style; it shows the French form of [[see:ancient]] without a T.
Like [[see:pageant]], it had no T in French, but English added one, as it did with [[see:ancient]].
Like [[see:parchment]], it had no T in French, but English added one, as it did with [[see:ancient]].
French itself added a T to form it, as it did with [[see:tyrant]], the same addition English made to [[see:ancient]].
French itself added a T to form it, as it did with [[see:peasant]], the same addition English made to [[see:ancient]].
The stake in a card game, related to [[same-root:ancient]] through the sense of before.
Related to [[same-root:ancient]] through the sense of before.
Called the old ancient wife in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, the first English record of [[see:ancient]], though she is Gawain's aunt or mother depending on the story.
Every pyramid, even unrelated ones in the Americas, is named after the Egyptian pyramids, through Greek [[from:pyramis]].
Greek word, probably Egyptian in origin, that gave [[gave:pyramid]]; the Greeks also used it for a presumably pyramid-shaped honey cake.
One of the few English words from Egyptian; it referred to the palace before the person, like the [[see:White House]], and was covered in their top 100.
Used to refer to the president's office, the hosts' comparison for how [[see:pharaoh]] went from the palace to the person living there.
From Arabic [[from:mumia]], an embalmed body; in English it first meant a medicinal substance made from Egyptian corpses, and mummies were eaten from the medieval period on.
From Greek [[from:sarkophagos lithos]], flesh-eating stone, from a limestone thought to help bodies decay; since 1705 it has meant an inscribed or carved stone coffin.
A suffix for something that eats something else, the same element as in [[same-root:sarcophagus]].
Shares the flesh element of [[same-root:sarcophagus]], as if the sarcastic are tearing at flesh.
A Greek word for a little spit or cooking skewer, given to the pointed monument; it is also the name of a printing symbol, like the [[see:asterisk]].
A keyboard symbol named after a star, which Rob found alongside the [[see:obelisk]] while researching typographical symbols.
Another name for the [[see:obelisk]] printing symbol, a tiny cross or dagger that dictionaries used to mark obsolete words.
From a Greek word meaning to squeeze, bind or embrace, after the Greek Sphinx; Susan Wise Bauer instead suggests Egyptian [[from?:shesep ankh]], living image.
The [[see:Sphinx]] asks what walks on four legs, then two, then three; the answer is a person, who crawls, walks and then uses a staff.
Answered the [[see:riddle of the Sphinx]] correctly, after which the Sphinx died, but it only led him to sleep with his mother.
Egyptian sphinxes with male pharaohs' heads and wingless lion bodies, royal or temple guardians unrelated to the Greek [[see:Sphinx]].
A [[see:stele]] found in 1799 at Rashid, which the French called [[from:Rosetta]]; its decree for [[see:Ptolemy V]] in hieroglyphs, [[see:Demotic]] and Greek enabled decipherment.
A later Egyptian script for the Egyptians' day-to-day language, used in the middle section of the [[see:Rosetta Stone]].
Greek for a standing block or slab; the [[see:Rosetta Stone]] is a broken piece of one.
The king praised in the [[see:Rosetta Stone]] decree; Ptolemy was the first word [[see:Jean-François Champollion]] worked out, from a [[see:cartouche]].
The French name for Rashid, the Egyptian town where the stone was found in 1799, which gave its name to the [[gave:Rosetta Stone]].
Had a good go at deciphering the [[see:Rosetta Stone]] before [[see:Jean-François Champollion]] made the breakthrough.
One of those who tried to decipher the [[see:Rosetta Stone]] before [[see:Jean-François Champollion]].
A 19th-century philologist who deciphered hieroglyphs from the [[see:Rosetta Stone]], using royal names in [[see:cartouche]]s and showing that signs could represent sounds.
The loop around royal names in hieroglyphs; a doublet of [[same-root:cartridge]], from French cartouche, a pistol charge, ultimately from Latin and Italian for a roll of paper.
Unpronounced hieroglyphs showing the theme of a word, like drawing a gift or a clock beside [[see:present]].
A doublet of [[same-root:cartouche]]; it went from cartouche to cartage to cartridge, so its R is unetymological.
The right term, not [[see:hieroglyphics]], says Ilona Regulski; signs stand for words, sounds or themes and face the start of the line; Rob made a video about them.
According to Egyptologist Ilona Regulski, this is the wrong word for the signs, which should be called [[see:hieroglyphs]].
Rob's example of how [[see:classifiers]] work: a drawn gift or clock beside it would show which sense was meant.
Writing words with pictures of things whose sounds make them up, as some hieroglyphs do, like writing [[see:belief]] with a bee and a leaf.
An example of the [[see:rebus principle]]: it could be written as a drawing of a bee next to a drawing of a leaf.
A hieroglyph representing one consonant sound, alongside the [[see:biliteral sign]] and the [[see:triliteral sign]].
A hieroglyph representing two consonant sounds, alongside the [[see:uniliteral sign]] and the [[see:triliteral sign]].
A hieroglyph representing three consonants at once, like the [[see:scarab beetle]], which can write [[see:kheper]].
Its hieroglyph can mean scarab or stand for the consonants of [[see:kheper]], because the Egyptian word for scarab had those consonants.
An Egyptian verb meaning to become, happen, develop or create, written with the [[see:scarab beetle]], a [[see:triliteral sign]].
The Egyptian word for brick that gave [[gave:adobe]]; its eh vowels are only Egyptologists' placeholders, since the real vowels are unknown.
From Egyptian [[from:djebet]], brick, via Arabic and Spanish, reaching English from Spanish speakers in the Americas; it names the brick, its material and such buildings.
The hosts wonder whether the software company named itself after [[see:adobe]] because you build things with its software.
A 22-letter consonantal script from [[from:Proto-Canaanite]] and [[from:Proto-Sinaitic]], ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic and Cyrillic writing; named from Greek [[from:phoinix]].
Early writing that, like [[see:Proto-Sinaitic]], adapted Egyptian hieroglyphic pictures into marks for Semitic sounds and gave rise to [[gave:Phoenician]].
Early writing that, like [[see:Proto-Canaanite]], adapted Egyptian hieroglyphic pictures into marks for Semitic sounds and gave rise to [[gave:Phoenician]].
The letter meaning house, from the house hieroglyph, which became the letter B; with [[see:aleph]], ox, it means we all write in ox house.
The letter meaning ox, whose ox's head was rotated to give A; also the first letter of the old Arabic order behind [[gave:abjad]].
A script focusing on consonants, like [[see:Phoenician]] and Arabic, named after the first four letters of the old Arabic order: [[from:aleph]], [[from:ba]], [[from:gimel]], [[from:dal]].
The Greek word for the Phoenicians, purple and red dyes and the date palm, which gave [[gave:Phoenician]]; it may be related to [[same-root?:phoenix]].
A Greek word that looks like [[same-root?:phoinix]] and may or may not be related to it or to its colour sense.
Means wedge-shaped, from Latin [[from:cuneus]], wedge, from reed marks pressed into clay; used from about 3200 BC to the 1st century AD, centred on [[see:Mesopotamia]].
The time before writing, so history begins about when [[see:cuneiform]] does.
A king of Uruk who, in a story from about 1800 BC, invented [[see:cuneiform]] to help his messenger remember messages to the lord of [[see:Aratta]].
A mythical city far to the east whose lord, in the [[see:Enmerkar]] story, was baffled by a cuneiform tablet and forced to submit.
Signs that each represent a syllable, which later [[see:cuneiform]] began to use.
One of the earliest works in [[see:cuneiform]], written in Akkadian, like the [[see:Epic of Gilgamesh]].
One of the earliest works in [[see:cuneiform]], written in Akkadian, like the [[see:Code of Hammurabi]].
The centre of [[see:cuneiform]]; the name literally means the area between two rivers, the [[see:Euphrates]] and the [[see:Tigris]].
A script found by [[see:Arthur Evans]] at [[see:Knossos]] in 1900, partly deciphered fifty years later by [[see:Michael Ventris]] through place names.
A British man who found hundreds of [[see:Linear B]] inscriptions at [[see:Knossos]] in Crete in 1900, believing they recorded the [[see:Minoans]]' language.
A palace in Crete where the Minotaur supposedly lived and [[see:Linear B]] was found; finding its name in the script was key to deciphering it.
Named after King [[from:Minos]], who had the Minotaur; [[see:Arthur Evans]] believed [[see:Linear B]] represented their language.
Deciphered [[see:Linear B]] through place names, comparing Cretan, mainland Greek and Cypriot texts until he located [[see:Knossos]].
An undeciphered script, some of whose signs closely resemble pictograms on the [[see:Phaistos Disc]].
A spiral disc of pictograms found nowhere else, a few resembling [[see:Linear A]]; proposed decipherments contradict each other and cannot be corroborated.
Not ancient: an illustrated plant book carbon-dated to the 1400s, in an unknown script, maybe a cipher or hoax, supposedly found by [[see:Wilfrid Voynich]].
A Polish bookseller who supposedly found the [[see:Voynich Manuscript]] at a Jesuit college in Italy in 1912; some suggest he faked it.
